examples.text: Inertia is the natural tendency of an object to resist any change in its motion!
When you shake a ketchup bottle and suddenly stop your hand, the sauce keeps moving down because of inertia!
Newton's first law says an object at rest stays at rest, and a moving object keeps moving, unless an unbalanced force acts on it!
When all forces on an object are balanced (net force is zero), its motion doesn't change, according to Newton's first law!
Acceleration is any change in speed or direction! It happens when a vehicle speeds up, slows down, or turns.

With your teacher, use a low-friction cart on a level track. First keep mass fixed and compare measured pulls. Then keep the measured net force similar and change mass. Record velocity at equal time intervals and calculate acceleration; repeat each trial. Compare with a = Fnet/m. Friction and an uneven pull can affect results. Do not treat a steeper ramp as a pure mass test: the force changes too.

Did you know every action has a reaction?

Newton's third law says that for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction!
The action and reaction forces act on two different objects, which is why they do not cancel each other out!

Why does a fisherman lean back when pulling a net?

When a fisherman pulls the net, they pull on each other! He must lean back so the net doesn't drag him forward.
When a boatman pushes water backward with a paddle, the water pushes the boat forward—making it move!

Draw a book and table separately. Label the upward force of table on book and the equal downward force of book on table: an action–reaction pair on different objects. The book’s weight is Earth pulling the book; its partner is the book pulling Earth, not the table’s upward force.

A force diagram can represent action-reaction pairs by drawing arrows that show the direction and strength of each force on the two interacting objects.
An electric current flowing in a metal wire is really just electrons moving along together!
Closing a switch completes an electrical circuit, letting electrons flow through and light up a bulb!

Electric current is moving electric charge. In metal wires the moving charges are electrons; other materials can carry current through ions. Build only teacher-approved low-voltage battery circuits. Open the switch before changing connections, use correctly rated parts and stop if anything heats unexpectedly. Keep liquids away and never use wall outlets or exposed mains wires. A plastic covering is not permission to handle damaged electrical equipment.

With a teacher, draw and assemble a low-voltage battery, switch and lamp circuit. Keep the switch open while connecting. Put an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel across a lamp. Compare series and parallel loads, recording current and voltage as resistance changes. Never connect this experiment to a wall outlet.

Use a teacher-approved low-voltage kit. Keep resistor type fixed while changing the number of series or parallel loads; record battery voltage and total current. Next keep the loads fixed while changing the battery voltage within their ratings. Compare repeated readings. Discuss tradeoffs: a series path is simple but one open part interrupts all loads. Parallel branches allow separate operation but adding branches increases total current at fixed voltage, so the source and wires must be suitable.
Ohm's law says current in a circuit equals voltage divided by resistance! It's a simple math rule: I = V/R.

How do we draw a battery in a circuit diagram?

A cell is drawn as a long line (positive!) and a short line (negative!). Several cells in series? That's alternating long-short-long-short lines!

Electromagnetic waves are produced when an electric charge changes its motion or speeds up! This happens when electrons vibrate back and forth inside an antenna.

Vibrating electric charges can emit electromagnetic waves. In a wave traveling through empty space, the electric and magnetic fields oscillate perpendicular to its travel direction and to each other: a transverse wave. Unlike sound, it does not need matter to carry it.

Vibrating electric charges can emit electromagnetic waves. In a wave traveling through empty space, the electric and magnetic fields oscillate perpendicular to its travel direction and to each other: a transverse wave. Unlike sound, it does not need matter to carry it.
All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light! That is about 300,000 kilometers per second in a vacuum.

Radio waves have the lowest frequency in the entire electromagnetic spectrum!
From longest to shortest wavelength, the electromagnetic spectrum order is: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, and gamma!
In the spectrum order, microwaves sit right between radio waves and infrared!
From longest to shortest wavelength, the electromagnetic spectrum order is: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, and gamma!

Where do X-rays sit in the spectrum order?

They sit right between ultraviolet and gamma rays!
From longest to shortest wavelength, the electromagnetic spectrum order is: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, and gamma!
Gamma rays have the highest frequency in the entire electromagnetic spectrum!
Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength in the entire electromagnetic spectrum!

What happens to the wavelength when frequency goes up?

As frequency increases from radio to gamma rays, the wavelength gets shorter and shorter!
Radio waves are invisible helpers! They are a special part of the spectrum that carry signals for our radio, TV, and cellphones.

What can an X-ray machine see?

An X-ray machine is a medical tool that takes pictures of bones to check if any are broken!

Can radiation help sick people in hospitals?

Yes! Doctors use strong gamma rays from radioactive decay to target and kill cancer cells. They carefully measure it to fight the disease while protecting healthy body parts.
Ultraviolet light from the sun causes sunburn, which makes our skin turn red and get damaged!

Read a CDC radiation-health reference and record its date. X-rays and gamma rays are ionizing radiation and can damage cells. Radio waves are non-ionizing; their hazards differ. Ultraviolet exposure can damage skin and eyes. Harm depends on radiation type, intensity and exposure, so do not label every electromagnetic wave equally dangerous.

Why do we find the same ancient fossils on continents far apart?

Identical fossils of the same ancient plants and animals are found on far-apart continents, showing that these lands were once joined together!
The coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like puzzle pieces — a clue they were once joined!
The Appalachian Mountains of eastern North America link with the Scottish Highlands, showing these lands were once connected.
Because the plates move, the continents slowly drifted apart to where they are today!
Deep ocean trenches are topographical evidence of plate boundaries because they form where one plate slides beneath another!

In groups, compare official maps of Philippine trenches, earthquakes and volcanoes. Use matching map scales and read each legend and date. Trace clusters and compare them with mapped plate boundaries. A deep trench supports an interpretation of subduction; earthquake and volcanic belts add evidence. Mark where patterns agree and where data are missing. A local fault is not automatically the boundary of a major plate.

There are three plate boundaries: convergent — plates collide and one subducts or land crunches up; divergent — plates move apart and new crust forms; transform — plates slide horizontally past each other with no crust created or destroyed.
At a divergent boundary, two plates pull apart! Magma rises from below, cools down, and forms brand new crust.

What happens when plates crash into each other?

At a convergent boundary, plates push and collide! This creates tall mountains, deep trenches, and lots of earthquakes and volcanoes.

At a transform boundary, plates slide and grind past each other sideways! This rough rubbing often causes strong earthquakes.
Scientists know what lived in each era by studying fossils! These are found in different layers of rock.
Most fossils are found in sedimentary rock because the layers slowly bury the remains of plants and animals!
Scientists measure the age of the rocks around a fossil to find out how old it is, sometimes millions of years!

How do index fossils help scientists?

An index fossil comes from a widespread organism that lived for a short time. It acts as a guide to determine the age of its rock layer!
In an undisturbed stack of rock layers, the oldest layer sits at the bottom and the youngest is on top — that's the law of superposition!

Compare an undisturbed stack of sedimentary layers: lower layers formed before higher ones. Index fossils can correlate layers at different sites. These give relative order, not a numerical age. Radiometric dating of suitable minerals can estimate an age with uncertainty. If a fossil layer lies between volcanic ash dated at 100 and 90 million years, its age is bracketed between those ages. Relative order and numerical ages work together in the geologic time scale.
Scientists estimate Earth is about 4.54 billion years old, based on radiometric dating of the oldest known meteorites and moon rocks!

We currently live in the Holocene epoch, which started about 11,700 years ago right after the last Ice Age!
Scientists discover a rock's age using radioactive dating, which measures the decay of radioactive elements inside the rock!

When did the Mesozoic Era begin?

The Mesozoic Era began about 252 million years ago!
We are now in the Cenozoic era, the "Age of Mammals," which began 66 million years ago!
The geologic time scale organizes Earth's history into chunks: eons, eras, periods, and epochs — from the longest stretches down to the shortest!

Did you know some rocks are older than the dinosaurs?

Many rocks are millions of years old! They act like nature's diary, recording Earth's long history.
The Lehmann discontinuity is the boundary between the liquid outer core and solid inner core, found by studying P-wave behavior!
Body waves travel through Earth's interior, and they include primary waves and secondary waves that move at different speeds.

How do scientists know the outer core is liquid?

S-waves cannot pass through liquid! Since they stop at the outer core, it proves the outer core is liquid.

How do scientists know Earth has a liquid outer core?

S waves (transverse seismic waves) cannot pass through liquid! After earthquakes, the absence of S waves in certain zones proved that Earth has a liquid outer core.
Deep inside our planet, iron is the main element that makes up Earth's core!
We can't drill deep into the Earth, so scientists use earthquake seismic waves like an x-ray to see the layers inside!
The Earth's crust is very thin, averaging only about 5 to 70 kilometers in thickness!
Planet Earth is made of 4 main layers: the crust, the mantle, the outer core, and the inner core!
Every tectonic plate is made of Earth's rigid outer layer. This tough shell is called the lithosphere!

Use a USGS reference and scale 1 cm = 1,000 km: Earth’s radius is about 6.37 cm on paper. Mark the core boundary at about 2.9 cm depth and the inner core at about 5.15 cm depth; the outer core lies between. Add the thin crust above the mantle. In a separate mechanical overlay, label lithosphere as crust plus rigid uppermost mantle, and asthenosphere beneath it. These overlap the composition layers; do not add them as extra thicknesses.

A comet orbits around the Sun, just like the planets do!
An asteroid is made of rock and metal, while a comet is made of ice, dust, and rock!
A meteoroid is a cool rock floating in space that has not yet entered Earth's atmosphere!

What is a meteoroid?

A meteoroid is a small rock in space, before it enters Earth's atmosphere!

Where is the asteroid belt found?

Right between the planets Mars and Jupiter!
An asteroid is made of rock and metal, while a comet is made of ice, dust, and rock!
In 2006, Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet, no longer a regular planet!
Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt and is also considered a dwarf planet!

Where do asteroids and meteoroids come from?

Many are leftover pieces from when the Solar System formed billions of years ago!
In the early solar system, microscopic dust and ice collided and stuck together to form planetesimals in a process called accretion!

Why do some meteor showers happen at the exact same time every year?

It's because Earth passes through the same comet-debris path during each orbit!

Where do meteor showers like the Perseids and Leonids come from?

Meteor showers happen when Earth passes through a comet's debris trail! The Perseids in August come from Comet Swift-Tuttle, and the Leonids in November come from Comet Tempel-Tuttle.

NASA’s meteor reference explains recurring showers as Earth crossing streams of debris left along orbits, often by comets. Use the source to connect the yearly return to Earth’s orbit, not a star falling toward us. Visibility and strength vary with the debris, weather and sky conditions; a calendar date is not a guarantee of a bright display.
Many annual showers are visible from the Philippines! Some northern radiants sit lower, but a local astronomy club table is a super useful source.
The Hubble Space Telescope orbits above Earth's atmosphere, so it can see space super clearly!

Telescopes collect light; images and spectra help scientists study positions, temperatures and composition. Space telescopes avoid much of the atmosphere’s blurring and absorption. Probes travel near or land on targets and measure fields, particles or surfaces. Compare a telescope image of Saturn with Cassini’s close measurements: each instrument answers a different question. Record the mission, instrument, observation and source, not only the launch year.
The Cassini probe went on an epic space journey to explore the planet Saturn and its rings!

What shape is DNA?

DNA is shaped like a twisted ladder — scientists call it a 'double helix'!

Build a paper model of the DNA double helix: two sugar–phosphate backbones form the sides. Label the base-pair rungs A–T and C–G, then twist the ladder gently. The order of bases stores information; the model shows structure, not DNA’s actual size or all its chemical detail.

How many building blocks make up DNA?

DNA is built from just four bases: adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine — A, T, G, and C!

In human cells, chromosomes package DNA. Genes are stretches of DNA with instructions for functional products, often proteins. A child inherits chromosome sets from the biological parents, carrying versions of genes called alleles. These influence traits, but many traits involve several genes and the environment. A gene is not a promise of one fixed height or eye color.

What is a mutation?

A mutation is a change in DNA — it might do nothing, help, or hurt the living thing that has it!

A mutation changes DNA sequence; chromosome changes can affect larger pieces. The NHGRI mutation reference lists copying errors, mutagens and viral infection among possible causes. Some infectious agents can alter host DNA; this does not mean every infection causes an inherited mutation. Radiation and certain chemicals can also damage DNA.

What causes mutations in DNA?

Mutations can be caused by things like radiation and certain chemicals that damage DNA.

Use a reliable genetics textbook to compare beneficial, harmful and neutral mutation effects. A DNA change that does not alter a protein’s function may be neutral. Another can disrupt a needed function; another may improve survival in a particular environment. Classify effects using evidence about the organism and conditions, not the word mutation alone.
A mutation that lets a bacterium survive an antibiotic is beneficial for the microbe but harmful for a sick person, depending on whose survival!

Genetic diversity helps a species adapt to change and resist disease — when a small population loses much of it, the species becomes more fragile.
A wildlife corridor is a strip of connected habitat that lets animals move between separated forests, helping keep their genetic diversity healthy.

Why is an ecosystem with many species tougher?

When many different species do the same job — like many kinds of insects that pollinate flowers — there's a backup if one disappears. That's why ecosystems with many species are more stable than ones with only a few!

The outer electrons of atoms act like glue, joining them together to form substances!
Valence electrons are the electrons in an atom's outermost shell! They are the boss that decides how the atom will bond with other atoms.

Sodium has one valence electron from group 1. It does not match oxygen, which has six from group 16!

Why does oxygen have six valence electrons?

Oxygen's atomic number is eight! Two electrons fill the inner shell, leaving six as valence electrons in the outer shell.

The electron dot diagram for oxygen shows the symbol O with six dots around it, one for each valence electron.

What happens when an atom loses or gains an electron?

It becomes charged and is called an ion!
When an atom loses electrons, it becomes a positively charged ion called a cation! A great example is the sodium ion, Na⁺.
When an atom gains extra electrons, it becomes a negatively charged ion called an anion! A common example is the chloride ion, Cl⁻.
In an ionic bond, positive and negative ions pull toward each other because opposite electric charges attract!

Potassium chloride (KCl) is made of potassium (+1) and chloride (-1) ions in a one-to-one ratio!

What does the formula MgCl2 mean?

It tells you there is one magnesium ion and two chloride ions in the compound!
A single water molecule is made of exactly two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom!
A water molecule (H₂O) has two covalent bonds! This happens because the oxygen shares electrons with each of its two hydrogen atoms.

What is the secret chemical code for water?

H2O!
The chemical formula for carbon dioxide is CO2!

What atoms make up the chemical formula for ammonia?

The chemical formula for ammonia is NH3. This means it is made of one nitrogen atom and three hydrogen atoms!

How are ions arranged in table salt?

In NaCl, sodium and chloride ions form a repeating pattern called a crystal lattice — not separate molecules!

In a metallic bond, outer electrons move freely like a sea of electrons! This is why metals conduct electricity and heat so well.

In the sea-of-electrons model, positive metal ion cores are held together by delocalized electrons. Layers can slide while this attraction continues, helping explain malleability and ductility. Mobile electrons also carry electric current and transfer thermal energy. Metals differ; this model does not mean every metal bends equally easily.

Why are ionic compounds like salt so hard to melt?

They are hard solids with very high melting points because the pull between their opposite ions is super strong!
